label: Permits and approvals
title: Work on site (“{anchor}”) is scheduled, but permits and inspection approvals are not mentioned
why: Work started without the right permits can be stopped and must sometimes be undone. Approval lead times often exceed what the schedule assumes.
question: Which permits and inspections are required before “{anchor}”, and what is the lead time for each?
nextStep: List every permit and inspection with owner and lead time, and put them on the schedule ahead of the dependent work.
disproof: A permit, consent or inspection list covering the “{anchor}”.

justifications.irreversibility: Work built without approval may need demolition

label: Ground conditions / site survey
title: The documents mention “{anchor}”:  is planned but no ground investigation or site survey is referenced
why: Unexpected ground conditions are among the largest causes of cost overrun. Survey results should shape the design, not follow it.
question: What do the soil and site surveys say about “{anchor}”, and has the design been checked against them?
nextStep: Commission or locate the geotechnical report and confirm the foundation design uses it.
disproof: A geotechnical, soil or site-survey report referenced in the plan or budget.

justifications.irreversibility: Foundations cannot be changed after the pour
justifications.cost: Survey costs time and money but is standard

label: Weather and seasonal delay
title: Outdoor work (“{anchor}”) is scheduled without allowing for weather or seasonal delay
why: Weather-sensitive trades slip first and pull dependent work with them. Schedules without float turn each delay into a missed handover.
question: How many weather days does the schedule allow for “{anchor}”, and what happens to later trades if they are used?
nextStep: Add weather float to outdoor activities and check the critical path with it included.
disproof: Weather allowance, seasonal constraints or schedule float for the “{anchor}”.

label: Contingency and change control
title: The budget (“{anchor}”) has no stated contingency or process for changes
why: Construction costs move: variations, price rises and unknowns are normal. A budget without contingency forces mid-project funding conversations.
question: What contingency is held against the “{anchor}”, who can release it, and how are variations approved?
nextStep: Add a contingency line (commonly sized to project risk) and write a variation approval rule.
disproof: A contingency line, variation process or provisional sums in the budget or contract.

label: Utility connections
title: The design needs a “{anchor}” supply but connection lead times and capacity are not covered
why: Utility connections often take months and are outside the contractor's control. A late connection can idle a finished building.
question: Has the utility provider confirmed capacity and a date for the “{anchor}” connection?
nextStep: Apply for connections now and put the confirmed dates on the programme.
disproof: A utility application, capacity confirmation or connection date.

justifications.cost: Application is quick; lead time is the issue

label: Site safety planning
title: Higher-risk work (“{anchor}”) is planned but no safety plan or method statement is referenced
why: Safety failures carry human cost and legal exposure, and regulators can halt a site. Method statements must exist before the work starts.
question: Where are the risk assessments and method statements for “{anchor}”, and who approves them?
nextStep: Collect method statements for each high-risk activity and confirm approval before mobilisation.
disproof: A safety plan, risk assessment or method statement covering the “{anchor}”.
